name: Process Power

positioning.oneLineSummary: Tests whether an accumulated, embedded activity system creates material results that rivals cannot reproduce by copying visible practices.
positioning.productLabel: Process Power Lens — based on Hamilton Helmer's public 7 Powers materials
notAClaimOf: a documented best practice being inimitable

attribution.display: Based on Hamilton Helmer's public Process Power doctrine

neutralParaphrase: Process Power may exist when a material cost or product advantage emerges from a long-accumulated, embedded, interdependent activity system whose tacit knowledge, causal opacity, social structure, or replication time prevents rivals from reproducing the result. Ordinary operational excellence, a single procedure, or complexity without causal evidence is insufficient.

locator.value: Process Power section lines 236-256: embedded activities, tacit knowledge, materiality, opacity, time, and operational-excellence caveat
Official audio 00:44:27-00:46:40: Process Power and distinction from Scale Economies
Abstract: intrinsic ambiguity as necessary but insufficient and no simple complexity-ambiguity correlation

requiredConditions: A multi-activity system rather than one practice is identified.
The system produces a material measured cost or product Benefit.
Accumulation, tacitness, interdependence, opacity, or social complexity creates a replication Barrier.
Scale Economies and Cornered Resource explanations are separately tested.

requiredEvidence.description: Interdependent routines, feedback loops, decision rights, supplier and employee coordination, and accumulated learning.
Cost, quality, speed, yield, reliability, innovation, or customer outcome difference attributable to the activity system.
Time, experimentation, failure history, social embedding, causal ambiguity, and knowledge not transferable through manuals or hiring one person.
Competitor copying, consultant transfer, hiring, technology automation, staff turnover, and evidence that the outcome gap persists or decays.

decisionQuestions: Which interacting activities create the result, and how?
Is the outcome delta material after controlling for scale and input quality?
How long did the activity system take to accumulate?
Can a rival copy it with consultants, hiring, software, or capital?
Have replication attempts failed, and why?
Does tacitness also make the company unable to sustain or transfer its own capability?
positiveSignals: A mapped multi-activity system predicts measured superior outcomes.
The result persists after controlling for scale, equipment, and input resources.
Knowledge is distributed, socially embedded, and reinforced over many cycles.
Well-resourced competitors copy visible practices without matching outcomes.
The company can reproduce and renew the capability internally.
redFlags: Complexity or culture language substitutes for a causal activity map.
The claimed process is a standard industry practice.
One executive, consultant, tool, or supplier explains the result.
The Benefit disappears after controlling for scale or better inputs.
Internal tacitness prevents succession, transfer, or improvement.
disconfirmingEvidence: Competitors match the outcome after adopting documented practices.
Employee hiring transfers the capability quickly.
Automation or modular technology removes the accumulated learning advantage.
Performance deteriorates when one person leaves.
The activity system is complex but not causally related to superior outcomes.
contraindications: Do not label operational excellence as Process Power.
Do not use complexity as proof of causal ambiguity.
Do not confuse superior equipment or scarce talent with Process.
Do not double count fixed-cost learning as Scale Economies.

instructions: Map the interdependent activity system and hypothesized causal paths.
Measure outcome differences and control for scale and inputs.
Assess accumulation, tacitness, transferability, and internal renewal.
Review competitor replication attempts and technology-driven decay.
Conclude on observed, candidate, path, unsupported, or inapplicable Process Power.

sourceReliability.low: Only culture or complexity claims are available.
sourceReliability.medium: Activity maps and outcome data are available.
sourceReliability.high: Longitudinal causal evidence and observed failed replication converge.

evidenceStrength.low: No material outcome delta is attributed.
evidenceStrength.medium: Outcome and accumulation are supported but replication remains uncertain.
evidenceStrength.high: Material outcome, activity causality, accumulation, and durable replication Barrier are supported.

evidenceCoverage.low: Activity system or outcome is missing.
evidenceCoverage.medium: System and outcome are covered but controls or replication are incomplete.
evidenceCoverage.high: Activities, outcomes, controls, tacitness, time, replication, transfer, and decay are covered.

applicabilityConfidence.low: Performance depends on standard practices or discrete inputs.
applicabilityConfidence.high: An interdependent accumulated activity system materially drives economics.

judgmentConfidence.low: Only an operational-excellence label is supported.
judgmentConfidence.medium: Candidate Process Power exists with unresolved replication.
judgmentConfidence.high: Observed material activity-system Benefit and replication Barrier are supported.

promotionRequirements: Complete licensed Process Power chapter review.
Define causal controls and replication evidence by operating model.
Validate incremental utility beyond operational KPIs and scale.
empiricalQualifications: Causal ambiguity may be necessary in some models but is not sufficient.
Complexity need not produce ambiguity or superior outcomes.
Tacitness can impair the focal firm's own transfer, succession, and renewal.

rights.notes: Public interview doctrine and external formal research are neutrally paraphrased.
